newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Sandinistas challenge Nicaraguan vote results.
newsitem.headline: Sandinistas challenge Nicaraguan vote results.

text.p: The left-wing Sandinista Front late on Monday formally appealed the results of Nicaragua's Oct. 20 elections, won by Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance.

The Sandinistas added to weeks of post-electoral bickering by demanding new elections be held in the provinces of Managua and Matagalpa, and calling for a revision of the vote at polling stations in 13 provinces due to what it said was evidence of fraud.

The leftist party submitted a 646-page list of alleged irregularities, including missing vote tally sheets and "massive numerical inconsistencies," to the Supreme Election Council (CSE) for review. The CSE is the nations' highest electoral authority.

"Our appeal demonstrates that there were irregularities, that there was fraud, in the October 20 elections ... that there is no legal basis for the vote results that were given last Friday," Sandinista leader Rene Nunez told reporters.
Final results released on Friday gave Aleman an easy 51 to 37.7 percent win over former President and Sandanista leader Daniel Ortega.
Under Nicaraguan election law, the Sandinistas have three days from their petition to argue their case to the CSE, which will have five days subsequently to rule on the petition.

But the Sandinista rebellion against the elections appeared to have little hope of success as world leaders rallied to congratulate Aleman on Sunday for his victory, among them U.S. President Bill Clinton and all Central American leaders except from Belize.

While the possibility of a violent Sandinista reaction to the vote results appears small, there remains a lingering resentment among Sandinista activists who believe they were victims of Liberal fraud.

Ortega has bitterly criticised election officials for complicity in a fraud, and lashed out at Nicaragua's government, the Catholic Church and business community for "polarizing" the election campaign with their attacks on the Sandinistas.

While Ortega has little choice but to accept the legality of Aleman's win, he has said he will not accept its "moral legitimacy," and will use it as a "political IOU" against the new government, political analyst Carlos Chamorro said in the news magazine Confidencial.
Chamorro said the Sandinistas will keep their bases mobilised throughout the Aleman administration by labelling it a "tamalero" government. "Tamale" in Nicaragua is slang for thief.
The new president will take office on Jan. 10.
